title: LRU Cache Simulation

statement.md: A market-data gateway caches the last instrument definitions it served, with strict capacity: when the cache is full, the **least recently used** entry is evicted. Both reads and writes count as *use*. Simulate the cache and report the result of every read.

Operations: `PUT k v` sets key $k$ to value $v$ (evicting the LRU key if at capacity, and note that updating an existing key is *not* an eviction); `GET k` returns the current value of $k$ or `MISS` if absent. A `GET` refreshes recency, even on a miss it changes nothing.

inputFormat: First line: capacity $c$ ($1 \le c \le 10^5$) and operation count $t$ ($1 \le t \le 10^5$). Then $t$ operations, one per line.
outputFormat: One line per `GET`: the value, or `MISS`.
constraints: keys are short strings, values are integers
an O(1)-per-operation design exists and is expected at these bounds

examples.input:
2 7
PUT a 1
PUT b 2
GET a
PUT c 3
GET b
GET c
GET a
examples.explanation: GET a refreshes a; PUT c evicts b (LRU); GET b misses; GET c hits 3; GET a hits 1 (a was refreshed).

hints: A hash map plus a doubly-linked list gives O(1) everything, or in Python, `collections.OrderedDict` with `move_to_end`.
Eviction removes the *front* (oldest) end; both GET and PUT move/insert at the *back*.

editorial.md: The LRU contract needs, per operation: O(1) lookup (hash map), O(1) recency update (move a node to the newest end of an ordered structure), and O(1) eviction (pop the oldest end). A doubly-linked list keyed by a hash map is the classic composition; `OrderedDict` is exactly that structure with the same guarantees.

The two behaviours tests love: an `UPDATE` of an existing key does not evict (the key stays, refreshed), and a `GET` on a present key refreshes it, changing which key the *next* eviction removes. Both are one-line differences in a correct implementation and silent bugs in a naive one.
